findings.claim: The more speculative long-term risks — AI systems acting against human interests — are taken seriously by researchers at labs like Anthropic and DeepMind, and are an active area of safety research.
findings.issue: Accurate and uncontroversial, but naming only Anthropic and DeepMind could read as selective; OpenAI and others also run prominent safety research programs. Not an error — just slightly narrow framing for a 'labs like' example. No change required.

findings.claim: Image caption: 'Image created with Google Gemini Pro'
findings.issue: Not a factual-accuracy problem (it's a tool attribution, and 'Gemini Pro' is still a current product-family name). Flagging only because if the site wants precision, Google's current Pro-tier flagship as of 2026 is Gemini 3.1 Pro; the generic 'Gemini Pro' label is fine and not stale.

findings.claim: Import AI — Jack Clark, co-founder and Head of Policy at Anthropic.
findings.issue: Stale title presented as current. Jack Clark changed roles in March 2026; he is now Anthropic's Head of Public Benefit (leading the Anthropic Institute), having previously held the title Head of Policy from 2021 to early 2026. He remains a co-founder. The draft presents the superseded 'Head of Policy' title as his current role. Suggested fix: 'co-founder and Head of Public Benefit at Anthropic' (or historically frame it).

newData.body:
A curated collection of the best places to learn more about AI, large language models, and the broader landscape. ### **Foundational Reading**

Attention Is All You Need — Original Transformer Paper

The 2017 Google research paper that introduced the Transformer architecture which underpins every modern LLM.

AcademicArchitecture

arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 ↗

The Illustrated Transformer — Jay Alammar

The clearest visual explanation of how transformers work. Essential reading for anyone wanting to understand the mechanics without heavy maths.

VisualBeginner-friendly

jalammar.github.io ↗

Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3 Paper)

OpenAI's landmark 2020 paper introducing GPT-3 and the concept of few-shot learning at scale.

AcademicOpenAI

arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165 ↗
### **Courses & Interactive Learning**

fast.ai — Practical Deep Learning for Coders

Free, hands-on course that takes you from basics to building real neural networks. No heavy maths prerequisites.

FreeCoursePractical

course.fast.ai ↗

Andrej Karpathy — Neural Networks: Zero to Hero

YouTube series by former Tesla and OpenAI researcher. Builds a neural network from scratch in Python. One of the best free resources available.

FreeYouTubeCoding

YouTube Playlist ↗

DeepLearning.AI Short Courses

Short courses on LLMs, prompt engineering, RAG, and agents, taught by Andrew Ng and leading practitioners from labs and companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Many run about one to two hours. As of 2026-10-01, the course videos are free to watch, while the hands-on labs, graded assignments, and certificates require a paid DeepLearning.AI Pro membership (listed at $25/month billed annually, or $30/month billed monthly). Pro launched in late 2025 as an established product, so this is not a temporary free-access window — the free tier is the videos themselves. Ideal for non-technical learners who want to start with the videos.

Free videosCourseBeginner-friendly

learn.deeplearning.ai ↗
### **News & Commentary**

The Batch — DeepLearning.AI Newsletter

Weekly AI news and commentary from DeepLearning.AI, with a personal letter from Andrew Ng in every issue. It focuses on the realities of AI — what's actually happening and what it means — so readers can keep up without being misled by hype. Clear, balanced, and accessible for non-technical readers.

NewsletterWeekly

deeplearning.ai/the-batch ↗

Import AI — Jack Clark

Detailed weekly newsletter from Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic and, as of 2026-10-01, the company's Head of Public Benefit, where he leads the Anthropic Institute. (He previously served as Anthropic's Head of Policy before moving into the role in March 2026.) Covers research, policy, and the strategic AI landscape. Read it on his own site, which is the canonical home for the archive.

NewsletterResearch

jack-clark.net ↗

Simon Willison's Blog

Practical, technically sharp commentary on LLM developments — how they actually work, what they are good at, and where they fail. Written by an independent researcher and open-source maintainer.

BlogTechnical

simonwillison.net ↗
### **Model Playgrounds**

Ollama — Run models locally

Download and run open-weight models on your own computer. Free, private, no API costs.

FreeLocalOpen source

ollama.com ↗

Hugging Face — Model Hub

The GitHub of AI models. Browse, download, and test thousands of open models. Essential reference for the open AI ecosystem.

FreeModelsCommunity

huggingface.co ↗

findings.claim: OpenAI's current flagship family is GPT-5.6
findings.issue: GPT-5.6 is no longer the current flagship. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3-4, 2026 as its flagship model (1,050,000-token context, $10/$50 per 1M tokens), followed by GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on September 22, 2026, and most recently GPT-6.1 Sol. As of today (2026-10-01), GPT-6 Astra is the flagship and GPT-5.6 is a superseded, prior-generation family. This is exactly the pipeline's primary failure mode: a stale lineup presented as current.

findings.claim: API pricing runs from $5 input / $30 output per million tokens for Sol, $2.50 / $15 for Terra, and $1 / $6 for Luna.
findings.issue: These are launch-day (July 9, 2026) prices and are stale. On July 30, 2026 OpenAI cut Terra to $2/$12 and Luna to $0.20/$1.20 per 1M tokens. Additionally, as of September 2026 GPT-5.6 Sol carries a promotional price of $4/$20 (reportedly running at least through November 21, 2026) following an August 21, 2026 price reduction. Presenting launch pricing as current is incorrect.

findings.claim: a 1 million token context window
findings.issue: Multiple sources list the GPT-5.6 context window as 1,050,000 tokens rather than a round 1,000,000. 'Roughly 1 million' is acceptable as framing, but the precise figure is 1.05M.

findings.claim: a February 2026 knowledge cutoff
findings.issue: OpenAI's documentation reportedly lists the GPT-5.6 knowledge cutoff more specifically as February 16, 2026. 'February 2026' is consistent but less precise.

findings.claim: GPT-5.5 Instant remains the default for everyday chat ... Terra and Luna are available in Work, Codex, and the API
findings.issue: This ChatGPT product-surface/default-model description reflects the July 2026 state and is likely outdated given the subsequent GPT-6 Astra rollout, which became selectable for most paid ChatGPT users in September 2026. The specific current default model in ChatGPT could not be independently confirmed and should be re-verified before publication.

findings.claim: models: Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5 (presented as the current lineup)
findings.issue: This is a superseded lineup presented as current — exactly the pipeline's primary failure mode. Opus 4.8 was superseded by Claude Opus 5 (released July 24, 2026) and then Opus 5.5 (released ~September 22, 2026). Fable 5 was superseded by Fable 5.1 (released September 1, 2026). As of the current date (2026-10-01), Anthropic's current lineup is approximately Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, plus restricted-access Mythos 5.1. The most recent release is Claude Sonnet 5.5 (September 28, 2026). Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 are still current; Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 are not.

findings.claim: As of July 21, 2026, Claude Fable 5 is available globally ... Anthropic describes it as its most capable widely released model, sitting above the Opus tier
findings.issue: The 'as of July 21, 2026' snapshot is explicitly dated (so it satisfies the date house rule), but it is used to frame a now-stale state of the world as the model card's current description. By 2026-10-01, Fable 5 is no longer the most capable widely released model — Fable 5.1 (Sept 1, 2026) has superseded it, and Opus 5/5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 have all launched since. Presenting Fable 5 as the current flagship is stale. (Historical framing like 'As of July 21, 2026, Fable 5 was...' would be acceptable; the problem is this reads as the model's present-tense description.)

findings.claim: with a context window of up to 1 million tokens on its Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 models at flat per-token pricing
findings.issue: This reinforces the stale lineup by naming Opus 4.8 as a current context-window reference point; the current Opus tier is Opus 5/5.5. Separately, Opus 4.8's 1M context was not universal across platforms (e.g., it was capped at 200K on Microsoft Foundry), so 'up to 1 million' is defensible but the model reference is outdated. Sonnet 5's 1M context and $2/$10 pricing are correct and now standard.

findings.claim: US export controls imposed on June 12 were lifted on June 30 and access was restored on July 1
findings.issue: This chronology is accurate: the US imposed export controls on Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 12, 2026; the Commerce Department lifted them on June 30, 2026; and access was restored July 1, 2026. No correction needed — flagged only to confirm it checks out.

findings.claim: flat per-token pricing (Sonnet 5)
findings.issue: Sonnet 5 launched at introductory $2/$10 pricing (through Aug 31, 2026) that was scheduled to revert to $3/$15 but was subsequently made permanent at $2/$10. 'Flat per-token pricing' (meaning no long-context surcharge) is accurate for Sonnet 5, but the phrasing could be misread as pricing history. Minor.

findings.claim: Haiku 4.5 supports 200,000 tokens
findings.issue: Correct — Haiku 4.5 has a 200K-token context window. Confirmed; no change needed.

findings.claim: Current models: Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite
findings.issue: Stale lineup presented as current. As of 2026-10-01, the current Flash workhorse is Gemini 3.8 Flash (released Sept 2, 2026), which superseded 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, and 3.7 Flash. Gemini 3.5 Flash is a legacy/superseded Flash model, not the current one. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite is also superseded by Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (July 21, 2026). Gemini 3.1 Pro is still the correct Pro flagship (preview). Correct current lineup is approximately: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro (Preview), Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.

findings.claim: ...spanning the fast, efficient Gemini 3.5 Flash, the higher-intelligence Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the ultra-cheap Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite.
findings.issue: Presents a superseded state of the world as current. Gemini 3.5 Flash is no longer the current Flash model (superseded by 3.6/3.7/3.8 Flash), and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite has been replaced by Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. The description leads with and centers the stale 3.5 Flash as the headline Flash model.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.5 Flash ... scoring 55 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index
findings.issue: Benchmark number does not match a current, authoritative figure for this model and is attached to a superseded model. Published Intelligence Index scores are 56 for Gemini 3.7 Flash and 59 for Gemini 3.8 Flash; no current source corroborates a '55' score for Gemini 3.5 Flash. The headline capability claim is both unverified and tied to a stale model.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.5 Flash offers a 1 million-token context window
findings.issue: The 1M-token context figure is accurate across current Gemini models (3.8 Flash, 3.1 Pro, 3.5 Flash-Lite all support 1M tokens), so this particular sub-claim is not itself wrong — but it is attached to the superseded 3.5 Flash model and should be re-pointed to the current Flash model.

findings.claim: Grok 4.5 is the current flagship since its July 8, 2026 release.
findings.issue: Grok 4.5 has been superseded twice and is no longer the flagship. xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, and then Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026, which is the current flagship as of today (2026-10-01). This presents a stale model lineup as current — the pipeline's primary failure mode. The July 8, 2026 release date for Grok 4.5 is itself correct, but the 'current flagship' framing is wrong.

findings.claim: models: Grok 4.5 · Grok 4.3 · Grok 4.1 Fast
findings.issue: The lineup is stale and incorrect. The current flagship Grok 4.7 and the prior Grok 4.6 are both missing. Grok 4.1 Fast is not a current model — its API variants were retired on May 15, 2026, with slugs redirected to Grok 4.3. A current lineup should center on Grok 4.7 (flagship, 500K context, $2/$6), with Grok 4.6 and Grok 4.3 (1M context, $1.25/$2.50) as predecessors.

findings.claim: Below it sit Grok 4.3, the lower-cost 1M-context tier ... and Grok 4.1 Fast, a budget, high-throughput option with a 2M-token window.
findings.issue: This positions retired/older models beneath Grok 4.5 as if that is the live hierarchy. Grok 4.1 Fast is retired (May 15, 2026). The underlying specs are historically accurate (Grok 4.3 = 1M context, ~$1.25/$2.50; Grok 4.1 Fast = 2M context), but presenting these as the current tier structure below a stale flagship is misleading.

findings.claim: priced at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output
findings.issue: Accurate for Grok 4.5 (and coincidentally for the current Grok 4.7, which carries the same $2/$6 standard pricing). No correction needed to the numbers themselves, but note it is attributed to a model that is no longer the flagship.

findings.claim: 500K-token context window (Grok 4.5)
findings.issue: Correct for Grok 4.5 and also for the current Grok 4.7. No numeric error.

findings.claim: In April 2026, Meta Superintelligence Labs launched a new proprietary model, Muse Spark, as the engine behind Meta AI — a strategic pivot away from Llama as Meta's frontier effort
findings.issue: The framing is stale/incomplete in a way that misleads on the CURRENT state. Muse Spark was announced April 8, 2026, but the line has since iterated well past the draft: Muse Spark 1.1 (July 9, 2026), Muse Code agent, an OPEN-WEIGHT Muse Glimmer 30B (Apache 2.0) on/around August 10, 2026, and Muse Spark 1.3 (September 2, 2026), which is Meta's current frontier model. Critically, the draft also states Muse Spark is 'proprietary' and casts the pivot as a move to a closed frontier, but as of the draft's own publication date (2026-10-01) Meta has already returned to open weights with Muse Glimmer and announced Muse Spark 1.2 weights will be open-sourced — so describing the pivot as simply 'away from Llama' to a proprietary engine understates reality. Update to reflect Muse Spark 1.3 as current and the Muse line's mixed open/closed status.

findings.claim: Meta's Llama 4 family remains the most widely deployed open-weight AI ecosystem ... Llama 3.3 70B remains a widely-deployed practical text-only option.
findings.issue: Not factually wrong on its own, but the description presents the Llama 4 lineup (Maverick, Scout, Llama 3.3 70B) as the current state in sustained present tense, and the model card's top-level 'models' field lists ONLY Llama 4 Maverick, Scout, and Llama 3.3 70B. Because Meta's current frontier model is now Muse Spark 1.3 (Sept 2, 2026) and the open Muse Glimmer 30B exists, presenting the Llama-only lineup as the live/current picture — the single most common failure mode flagged — risks misleading readers. The Muse paragraph partially mitigates this, but the card header and framing should make clear Llama 4 is the last open LLAMA-branded generation, not Meta's current frontier.

findings.claim: In April 2026, Meta Superintelligence Labs launched a new proprietary model, Muse Spark
findings.issue: Specific date precision: multiple sources (TechCrunch, CNBC, VentureBeat, Meta newsroom) date the launch to April 8, 2026. 'In April 2026' is acceptable but an exact date would be stronger. Also note the model was initially consumer/app-facing with only a private API preview at launch, not broadly available as 'proprietary model' might imply.

findings.claim: though existing Llama models remain open and available for self-hosting via Ollama, Hugging Face, and every major inference framework
findings.issue: This is accurate (Llama 4 remains open-weight and downloadable), but the sentence sits under a description with no explicit 'as of <DATE>' qualifier anywhere in the card. Per the house rule, time-sensitive currency claims ('remains the most widely deployed', 'remains a widely-deployed practical option') should carry an explicit date. The card contains no 'as of <date>' statement at all; adding one (e.g., 'as of October 2026') is recommended, though the absence of a bare 'as of writing'/'as of today' means the strict BLOCKING trigger for that specific rule is not met.

findings.claim: Muse Spark 1.1 (current); models list: 'Muse Spark 1.1 (current), Muse Spark 1.0'
findings.issue: Stale lineup presented as current. As of today (2026-10-01), the current model is Muse Spark 1.3, released September 2, 2026; Muse Spark 1.2 shipped August 5, 2026. Muse Spark 1.1 (July 9, 2026) has been superseded twice. Also, the original model is 'Muse Spark' (April 8, 2026), not 'Muse Spark 1.0' — no release is documented under the name '1.0'. This is the pipeline's primary failure mode: a superseded lineup framed as the current one.

findings.claim: As of July 2026, the current model in this family is Muse Spark 1.1...
findings.issue: The 'as of July 2026' date is stale/misleading for content being published on 2026-10-01. It asserts a state of the world (current model = 1.1) that is no longer true. The current model as of publication is Muse Spark 1.3 (released 2026-09-02). The entire 'current model' framing must be updated to 1.3 or the content re-framed historically.

findings.claim: Muse Spark 1.1... now runs in 'Thinking' mode inside the Meta AI app and at meta.ai
findings.issue: Presented in present tense as the current consumer experience. Since 1.1, Meta has released 1.2 and 1.3, and 1.3 was rolling out to consumer surfaces (Instagram, Facebook, Meta AI). Stating 1.1 'now runs' in the consumer app describes a superseded state as current.

findings.claim: Meta released [Muse Spark 1.1] on July 9, 2026 as its second Meta Superintelligence Labs model
findings.issue: 'Second MSL model' is imprecise. MSL also released Muse Image (July 7/8, 2026), reported as the second major MSL release. Within the Muse Spark text line, 1.1 is the second Muse Spark version. The claim is defensible if scoped to the Muse Spark LLM line but could be read as counting all MSL models, where it would be inaccurate.

findings.claim: released on July 9, 2026... a significant upgrade over the original Muse Spark from April
findings.issue: Factually correct for 1.1 specifically (original Muse Spark debuted April 8, 2026), and the API/pricing/context-window details ($1.25 input, $4.25 output per million tokens, $20 free credits, US-only self-serve preview, 1M-token context) all check out for the 1.1 launch. No factual error in these historical details — they are only problematic because the surrounding text frames this past release as the current state.

modelCardResults.name: DeepSeek

findings.claim: models: "DeepSeek V4 Pro · DeepSeek V4 Flash" — presenting V4 Flash as a current model in the lineup
findings.issue: DeepSeek V4 Flash was retired on September 10, 2026, when DeepSeek released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (API ID 'deepseek-flash', a 552B-parameter MoE with native vision). The legacy deepseek-v4-flash ID now merely routes to V4.1 Flash. The card's two-model lineup therefore describes a superseded state as current and omits the actual newest model, V4.1 Flash. The lineup should be updated to 'DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · DeepSeek V4 Pro' (V4.1 Flash is current; V4 Pro remains served but is being wound down).

findings.claim: "DeepSeek V4 Pro is the current flagship" and "DeepSeek V4 Flash trades some capability for speed and even lower cost. Both are available as open weights and via the DeepSeek API."
findings.issue: This describes a stale state of the world as current. (1) V4 Flash is retired, not currently available as a distinct model. (2) DeepSeek's own announcement states tests put V4.1 Flash ahead of V4 Pro on performance, cost, speed and runtime, and that DeepSeek is phasing out V4 Pro; V4 Pro's 'flagship' status is being deprecated in favor of the new V4.1 architecture family. V4 Pro API service was kept alive after an originally-announced Sept 14 reroute was reversed, but the content's framing of a stable V4 Pro + V4 Flash pair as the current offering is no longer accurate.

findings.claim: The description text contains no explicit 'as of <date>' marker for a fast-moving, rapidly-changing claim about the current lineup.
findings.issue: House rule requires an explicit date for currency claims. The content asserts current-state facts ('is the current flagship', 'Both are available') without any dated qualifier. While there is no bare 'as of writing'/'as of today' phrase to trigger a hard block on that specific rule, the absence of a date on volatile currency claims is worth flagging; given DeepSeek's rapid release cadence, an explicit 'as of <date>' should be added.

findings.claim: "DeepSeek's January 2025 release of R1 shocked the AI industry by matching OpenAI o1's reasoning benchmark performance at a fraction of the training cost"
findings.issue: This historical claim is accurate and well-supported: R1 was released January 20, 2025 and performed on par with OpenAI o1-1217 on reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME 2024 79.8% vs o1's 79.2%; MATH-500 97.3%). No correction needed; included only to confirm it checks out.
